passages.title: The Night Journey to the Farthest Mosque
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah 17 opens with a burst of praise: *Subḥāna alladhī asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan* — "Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night." The whole night of al-Isrāʾ and al-Miʿrāj is folded into this single ayah, which names Allah as the Doer, the traveller as "His servant," and states the purpose: "that We might show him of Our signs." Ibn Kathir's comment is the key: **Allah glorifies Himself for His ability to do that which none but He can do**, for there is no god but He and no Lord besides Him. This is not first a travel report; it is a declaration about Allah, with the journey as the evidence.

## The words of the ayah

**Subḥān.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this word registers wonder or introduces a great marvel; Ibn Kathir says it is spoken "in the case of serious matters." Had this been merely a dream, there would have been nothing so astounding about it — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, any human being can dream that he went to the heavens.

**asrā … laylan.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *asrā* comes from *isrāʾ*, which literally means **to make someone travel at night**; *laylan* makes that sense unmistakable, and Ibn Kathir glosses it "in the depths of the night." Because *laylan* is left indefinite — "a night" rather than "the night" — only *part* of a night was spent. **Isrāʾ** is the journey from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it stands proved under the definitive textual authority of this very ayah; **Miʿrāj** is the journey from there to the seven heavens, which finds mention in the verses of Sūrah an-Najm and is proved by hadith appearing in uninterrupted succession.

**bi-ʿabdihi — "His servant."** On the greatest night of his life, Allah names the Prophet ﷺ simply *servant*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws three things from it. First, it is the highest honour, not a diminishment: when Allah on His own elects to call someone "His servant," a unique bond of love lies embedded in the word — compare *ʿibād ar-Raḥmān*, "and the servants of Ar-Raḥmān are those who walk on the Earth gently" (25:63). The highest achievement a person is capable of is to become a perfect servant of Allah; on this eve of special honour, out of all his attributes of perfection, the quality of ideal servitude is what was chosen. Second, it is a guard-rail: a journey full of extraordinary miracles could give someone the wrong impression of divinity — something like what happened with the Christians over the raising of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him). By saying *ʿabd*, it was declared that despite all those miracles the Prophet ﷺ was still a servant of Allah, not a god. Third, *ʿabd* is no word for a spirit all by itself; it names the combination of body and spirit.

## The two sanctuaries and the blessed land

Ibn Kathir: **al-Masjid al-Ḥarām** means the Masjid in Makkah; **al-Masjid al-Aqṣā** means the Sacred House in Jerusalem, "the origin of the Prophets from the time of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that on occasions the entire Ḥaram is also called by that name — which removes a conflict in the reports, some holding that he ﷺ set out from the home of Umm Hāniʾ and others from the Ḥaṭīm: he may have been at her house first, then walked over to the Ḥaṭīm and begun the journey from there.

Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī asked the Prophet ﷺ which masjid of this world came first; he said, "Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām," then al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, with forty years between them — adding that Allah has made the entire earth a masjid for us, so wherever the time of Ṣalāh comes, offer it right there (reported by Muslim). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites the early authority Mujāhid, that Allah made the site of the Baytullāh two thousand years before He made the earth, and that al-Masjid al-Aqṣā was built by Sulaymān (peace be upon him) — reported by an-Nasāʾī with sound chains from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, as quoted from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī.

In "**whose surroundings We have blessed**," the blessing spills outward from the mosque. Ibn Kathir reads it of the land's agricultural produce and fruits. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes *ḥawl* ("environs") as the entire land of Shām and distinguishes two kinds of blessing — **religious**, since it has been the qiblah of all past prophets, their home and their last resting place; and **worldly**, its land being green, lush and verdant with streams, rivers and fruit farms. It cites Muʿādh ibn Jabal's report that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah says: "O land of Syria, thou art My region chosen from many and I shall make My chosen servants reach thee" (from Qurṭubī).

## "that We might show him of Our signs"

Ibn Kathir: these are **great signs**, as Allah says elsewhere, "Indeed he did see of the greatest signs of his Lord" (53:18).

**The mount.** Imam Ahmad reported from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Al-Burāq was brought to me, and it was a white animal bigger than a donkey and smaller than a mule. One stride of this creature covered a distance as far as it could see. I rode on it and it took me to Bayt al-Maqdis, where I tethered it at the hitching post of the Prophets. Then I entered and prayed two Rakʿahs there, and came out." (This version was also recorded by Muslim.)

**The heart opened.** In Abū Dharr's report (Al-Bukhari), Jibrīl came down and opened his chest and "washed it with Zamzam water," then poured into it a vessel of gold filled with wisdom and faith.

**The drink offered.** In Anas's report (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by Muslim), Jibrīl brought him a vessel of wine and a vessel of milk, and he chose the milk; Jibrīl said, "You have chosen the Fiṭrah" — the natural instinct a human being is created upon. Abū Hurayrah's narration gives the choice its edge: he was told, "You have been guided to the Fiṭrah — or — You have chosen the Fiṭrah. If you had chosen the wine, your Ummah would have gone astray" (Al-Bukhari and Muslim).

**The ascent.** Anas's report (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by Muslim) takes him heaven by heaven. At each one Jibrīl asked for it to be opened and was questioned — "Who are you?" "Jibrīl." "Who is with you?" "Muhammad." — and then it was opened. In the first he saw Ādam; in the second "the two maternal cousins, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā"; in the third Yūsuf, "who had been given the beautiful half"; in the fourth Idrīs, at whose mention the Prophet ﷺ said, Allah says, "And We raised him to a high station" (19:57); in the fifth Hārūn; in the sixth Mūsā; and in the seventh Ibrāhīm, "leaning back against the Much-Frequented House (al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr). Every day seventy thousand angels enter it, then they never come back to it again." Of each of the prophets: he "welcomed me and prayed for good for me."

In Abū Dharr's report (Al-Bukhari), Ādam sat "with a multitude to his right and another to his left. When he looked to his right he smiled, and when he looked to his left, he wept" — Jibrīl explained that these were the souls of his descendants, the people of Paradise on his right and the people of Hell on his left. And in Mālik ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah's report (Imam Ahmad), when the Prophet ﷺ passed Mūsā, Mūsā wept, and when asked why, said: "I am weeping because a young man was sent after me and more people from his Ummah than from mine will enter Paradise."

**The far horizon.** He was taken to *Sidrat al-Muntahā*, the Lote tree beyond which none may pass. In Anas's report (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by Muslim), "its leaves were like the leaves [ears] of elephants and its fruits were like jugs, and when it was veiled with whatever it was veiled with by the command of Allah, it changed, and none of the creatures of Allah can describe it because it is so beautiful." In Al-Bukhari's version, he was taken up "until I reached a level where I could hear the sound of the pens" — Ibn Kathir explains these as the pens of destiny, which write down what is decreed to happen.

**And warnings.** Anas reported him saying: "When I was taken up to my Lord, I passed by people who had nails of copper with which they were scratching their faces and chests. I asked, 'Who are these, O Jibrīl?' He said, 'These are those who ate the flesh of the people [i.e., backbiting] and slandered their honor'" (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by Abū Dāwūd).

## The gift of the night: the five prayers

In Anas's report (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by Muslim): "Then Allah revealed that which He revealed to me. He enjoined on me fifty prayers every day and night." On the way down Mūsā stopped him: "Go back to your Lord and ask Him to reduce (the burden) for your Ummah, for your Ummah will not be able to do that. I tested the Children of Israel and found out how they were." Again and again he returned, and each time it was reduced by five, "until He said, 'O Muhammad, these are five prayers every day and night, and for every prayer there is (the reward of) ten, so they are (like) fifty prayers.'" In the version recorded by Al-Bukhari: "They are five but equal in reward to fifty, for My word does not change."

When Mūsā urged one more return, the Prophet ﷺ answered — in Mālik ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah's report (Imam Ahmad) — "I have asked my Lord until I feel too shy. I accept this and submit to Him." Then a voice called out: "My order has been decreed and I have reduced the burden on My servants." (Similar narrations were recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.)

Ibn Kathir: in this is "a strong indication of the greatness and virtue of the prayers"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "This shows the importance and merit of Ṣalāh as being the foremost out of all acts of ʿIbādah." Ibn Masʿūd added that on that night the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "was given the five prayers and the final Ayat of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and forgiveness was granted for major sins to those who do not associate anything in worship with Allah" (Al-Bayhaqī; recorded by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ). And note Mūsā's part in it: hard experience of his own people, spent on someone else's Ummah.

## Leading the prophets

Ibn Kathir: at al-Masjid al-Aqṣā "the Prophets all gathered there, and he ﷺ led them in prayer in their own homeland. This indicates that he is the greatest leader of all." Abū Hurayrah described the gathering — Mūsā, ʿĪsā and Ibrāhīm each standing in prayer — "then the time for prayer came, and I led them in prayer" (Muslim).

Ibn Kathir notes that some reports say this prayer happened when he first entered, before the ascent, but holds it more likely that it was after he came back — because when he passed the prophets in the heavens he asked Jibrīl about them one by one, which would have been unnecessary had he already led them all. He adds that he was first required to come before the Divine Presence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows the same reasoning: then the prophets came down with him as far as Bayt al-Maqdis to see him off, and by Jibrīl's signal that he step forward to lead the prayer, his precedence over them was demonstrated in practice. Then he departed riding Burāq and reached Makkah while it was still dark.

**Did he see his Lord?** ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaqīq relates that Abū Dharr asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ exactly that. In Muslim's wording the answer was: "(I saw) a light, how could I see Him?" The sources give that and no more.

## The morning after: denial, and a title earned

Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās reported the Prophet ﷺ saying: "On the night when I was taken on the Night Journey, I woke up in Makkah the next morning having anxiety that, I knew that the people would not believe me." He kept away from people until Abū Jahl came to sit with him, asking mockingly, "Is there anything new?" When he ﷺ said he had been taken to Bayt al-Maqdis that night and was among them again by morning, Abū Jahl called out, "O people of Banī Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy!" and had him repeat it before the gathering. "They began to clap their hands together and put their hands on their heads in astonishment at this 'lie' — as they claimed it to be." Then some among them who had travelled to that land and seen the sanctuary said: "Can you describe the sanctuary to us?" He ﷺ said: "I started to describe it, until I reached a point where I was not sure about some of the details, but then the sanctuary was brought close and placed near the house of ʿUqayl — or ʿIqāl — so I could look at it and describe the details." The people said, "As for the description, by Allah he has got it right." (Recorded by An-Nasāʾī and Al-Bayhaqī.)

It cost some people their faith. Imam Ahmad records from Ibn ʿAbbās that when he came back and told them about the journey, the features of Bayt al-Maqdis and the caravan of Quraysh, "some people said, 'We do not believe what Muhammad is saying,' and they left Islam and became disbelievers."

And it gained one man his name for ever. Al-Bayhaqī records that some people from Quraysh went to Abū Bakr and said, "Have you heard what your companion is saying? He is claiming that he went to Bayt al-Maqdis and came back to Makkah in one night!" Abū Bakr said, "Did he say that?" They said, "Yes." He said, "Then I bear witness that if he said that, he is speaking the truth." They pressed him, and he answered, "Yes, I believe him with regard to something even more than that. I believe him with regard to the revelation that comes to him from heaven." From then on, says the report, Abū Bakr was known as **aṣ-Ṣiddīq**.

## Body and soul, awake — not a dream

Ibn Kathir assembles the evidence: the words **"Subḥān Allah,"** which "are spoken in the case of serious matters"; the **reaction** of Quraysh, who would not have hastened to call him a liar, and the group who had become Muslims who would not have deserted the faith over a dream; the word **ʿabd**, which "refers to both soul and body"; **17:60**, "And We made not the vision which we showed you but a trial for mankind," which Ibn ʿAbbās said is what the Messenger ﷺ saw **with his own eyes** during the Night Journey (recorded by Al-Bukhari); **53:17**, "The sight turned not aside, nor did it transgress" — and sight is a physical faculty, not a spiritual one; and **al-Burāq**, since "the soul does not need a means of transportation of this nature."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that when the Prophet ﷺ related the event to Umm Hāniʾ she advised him not to mention it to anyone, or people would falsify it all the more — hardly a worry over a dream. It also handles the dream-reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿĀʾishah fairly: according to the majority of Muslim scholars, *ar-ruʾyā* in 17:60 means *seeing*; and even if the word is taken in the sense of a dream, it is not far-fetched that a spiritual Miʿrāj in the form of a dream took place before or after the physical one, so that what is reported from them "is also correct in its place — but it does not necessarily imply that physical Miʿrāj did not take place."

On transmission: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir named twenty-five Companions from whom these reports come — among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Dharr, Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, Umm Hāniʾ and ʿĀʾishah. Al-Ḥāfiẓ ʿUmar ibn Diḥyah said the reports of the hadith of the Isrāʾ "reach the level of *Mutawātir*" (mass-transmitted), and Qurṭubī likewise holds the narrations recurrent and uninterrupted. Ibn Kathir's conclusion, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes it: "As for the Hadith of al-Isrāʾ, there is a consensus of all Muslims on it. Only heretics and atheists have denied it."

**When did it happen?** Ibn Kathir reports Mūsā ibn ʿUqbah, narrating from az-Zuhrī, that the Isrāʾ happened one year before the Hijrah — also ʿUrwah's opinion — while as-Suddī said sixteen months before it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, surveying Qurṭubī, adds several more views — six months before the Hijrah, five years after the call to prophethood, eighteen months after it, and al-Ḥarbī's dating to the night of the 27th of Rabīʿ ath-Thānī one year before the Hijrah. Its conclusion is that the hadith scholars did not follow these up with any decisive statement, while "as commonly known, the 27th night of the month of Rajab is the Night of Miʿrāj — and Allah, the Pure and the High, knows best."

## "Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing"

Ibn Kathir: **He hears all the words of His servants, believers and disbelievers, faithful and infidel, and He sees them and gives each of them what he deserves in this world and the Hereafter.** On the morning after, the clapping, the sneering and Abū Bakr's quiet "then he is speaking the truth" were all heard by Him and seen by Him.

## Living it

- **Guard the five prayers.** Both commentaries read the fifty-reduced-to-five as a proof of Ṣalāh's rank above every other act of worship.
- **Fear backbiting.** Jibrīl's identification of the people tearing their faces and chests with nails of copper was plain: "those who ate the flesh of the people and slandered their honor."
- **Choose the milk.** He took the vessel of *fiṭrah*; of the other he was told, "If you had chosen the wine, your Ummah would have gone astray."
- **Learn Abū Bakr's logic.** He weighed the claim not against his sense of the possible but against the one who made it.
- **Aim at servanthood.** The word Allah chose for him on his highest night was *ʿabd*. Whatever else a believer wants to become, that is the summit.

passages.title: Israel's scripture and two cycles of corruption
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing**

Sūrah al-Isrā' opens with the Prophet ﷺ carried by night to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā. Ayat 2–8 then tell the story of that sanctuary's own people: a Book given to Mūsā, a covenant to rely on Allah alone, a warning written into that very Book that its holders would twice tear up the land, and the two devastations that followed. What binds the passage into one unit is a single principle, stated in ayah 7 — *if you do good, you do good for your own selves; if you do evil, it is against yourselves* — first illustrated by history, then left standing over every later generation in ayah 8.

## Why Mūsā, immediately after the Night Journey

Allah has just mentioned how He took His servant Muhammad ﷺ on the Journey by Night, and follows it at once with Mūsā — "His servant and Messenger who also spoke with Him." Allah, Ibn Kathir observes, often mentions Muhammad and Mūsā together, and the Tawrah and the Qur'an together. The Messenger carried to Jerusalem is set beside the Messenger whose people were entrusted with it — one chain, one message, one law of consequence running through both.

## Ayah 2: a Book, and only one Wakīl

"And We gave Mūsā the Scripture" — meaning the Tawrah, says Ibn Kathir — "and made it," that is, the Scripture, "a guidance," that is, a guide, "for the Children of Israel." Then comes the purpose of the whole gift: *that you take no wakīl besides Me*. Ibn Kathir reads the construction as "lest they should take" — the Book was given precisely so that they would not.

A **wakīl** is the one to whom you hand your affairs: the trustee, the agent who manages what you cannot manage yourself, the back you lean against. Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct — "you have no protector, supporter or god besides Me." Notice how much wider that is than a ban on carved idols: it reaches whatever a frightened heart actually leans on — a patron, an army, an arrangement. And Ibn Kathir anchors it: Allah revealed to every Prophet that he should worship Him alone, with no partner or associate. The Tawrah, at its root, was saying what the Qur'an says.

## Ayah 3: "children of those We carried with Nūḥ"

Instead of naming their own lineage, Allah addresses them by the ark. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is reminding them of blessing — as if to say: *O descendants of those whom We saved and carried in the ship with Nūḥ, follow in the footsteps of your father.* Every one of them exists only because Allah kept one boat afloat. That is the ground on which ayah 2's demand rests.

Which of the father's traits are they told to imitate? Not his endurance, not his long preaching — **"Verily, he was a grateful servant"** (*'abdan shakūrā*).

Ibn Kathir shows how small the door of that gratitude is. Imam Ahmad reported that Anas ibn Mālik said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah will be pleased with His servant if, when he eats something or drinks something, he praises Allah for it."* This was also recorded by Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasā'ī. Mālik said of Zayd ibn Aslam that "he used to praise Allah in all circumstances."

And that title outlives Nūḥ. Al-Bukhārī mentioned the ḥadīth of Abū Zurʿah from Abū Hurayrah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said, *"I will be the leader of the sons of Adam on the Day of Resurrection…"* — and in it, when the crowds seek intercession, they come to Nūḥ saying: *"O Nūḥ, you were the first of the Messengers sent to the people of earth, and Allah called you grateful servant, so intercede for us with your Lord."* On the Day when every reputation is stripped away, the description people appeal to is the one Allah gave him in ayah 3.

Ibn Kathir adds a second layer to the reminder: alongside the memory of the ark, "Remember the blessing I have granted you by sending Muhammad."

## Ayah 4: a decree announced in advance

*"And We decreed for the Children of Israel in the Scripture: indeed you would do mischief in the land twice, and you would become tyrants, extremely arrogant."*

Ibn Kathir explains the verb *qaḍaynā* as: Allah had already told them, in the Book He revealed to them, what would happen — proving the usage from another ayah, "And We made known this decree to him, that the root of those sinners was to be cut off in the early morning" (15:66), where it plainly means *We informed him of it beforehand*. So ayah 4 is not a fate forced on them; it is a warning delivered to them, in writing, before either disaster came.

Note the two things foretold. The first is *fasād* — corruption that spreads, spoiling the land, not merely private sin. The second, "extremely arrogant," means in Ibn Kathir's words that "they would become shameless oppressors of people." Ruin of the land and contempt for people arrive together.

## Ayah 5: the first cycle

*"So when the promise came for the first of the two, We sent against you servants of Ours given to terrible warfare. They entered the very innermost parts of your homes. And it was a promise fulfilled."*

Ibn Kathir: "We unleashed soldiers against you from among Our creatures who were given to terrible warfare" — men of great strength, weapons and power. They took possession of the land and "invaded the very innermost parts of your homes, going between and through your houses, coming and going freely with no fear of anyone." The chilling detail is the loss of the last private space. Then the seal: *"a promise fulfilled."* What was written in ayah 4 was not rhetoric; it was carried out to the letter.

**A word chosen with precision.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Allah calls these invaders *'ibādan lanā* — "some servants belonging to Us" — and not *'ibādanā*, "Our servants." In ayah 1, when Allah honoured the Prophet ﷺ, He named him simply *'abdihi*, "His servant" — the highest station a human being can reach being that Allah calls him His own. Here the men doing the punishing were disbelievers, so the attribution is deliberately loosened: every human being is Allah's servant by creation, but for want of faith these are not the accepted servants who can be attached directly to Him.

**Who were they?** Ibn Kathir states frankly that "the earlier and later commentators differed over the identity of these invaders." Many *Isrā'īliyyāt* — reports taken from Jewish sources — were narrated about this, and he refuses to lengthen his book with them: some are fabricated, "concocted by their heretics," and others may be true, "but we have no need of them, praise be to Allah. What Allah has told us in His Book is sufficient… Neither Allah nor His Messenger required us to refer to them." Where Allah leaves a name out, the name was not the point.

What he does affirm is the moral shape of the event: when they committed transgression and aggression, Allah gave their enemies power over them — and "their humiliation and subjugation was a befitting punishment, and your Lord is never unfair or unjust to His servants." They had rebelled and killed many of the Prophets and the scholars.

Ibn Jarīr recorded from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd that he heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib say that Nebuchadnezzar conquered ash-Shām, destroying Jerusalem and killing its people. Ibn Kathir judges the report authentic from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib — that is, it is Saʿīd's own report of past history, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ — and the event well known: Nebuchadnezzar killed their nobles and scholars, "did not leave alive anyone who knew the Tawrah by heart," and took many captives from the sons of the Prophets. Note what perished with the scholars — the memory of the Book itself.

## The two cycles in history

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the record. It counts six such episodes in the history of Bayt al-Maqdis, of which the Qur'an mentions two: a plundering by a ruler of Egypt after the death of Sulaymān, peace be upon him, when the ruler of Bayt al-Maqdis had turned irreligious and corrupt; a second Egyptian attack some four centuries later, after idol-worship and infighting set in; Nebuchadnezzar's first conquest of the city; then his return, when he killed, destroyed property on a huge scale and burned the city to rubble, and the people went into seventy years of exile in Babylon — until the King of Iran conquered Babylon, showed the exiles mercy, sent them home with the property that had been looted from them, and they, now repentant, restored al-Masjid al-Aqṣā with his support; then, once peace and prosperity returned and the old sins with them, an attack in which forty thousand were killed and forty thousand taken as prisoners and slaves; and finally, forty years after the raising of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, the Roman destruction of city and Masjid under a king called Titus, after which the Masjid lay desolate until Sayyidnā ʿUmar had it reconstructed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is honest that it is "difficult to precisely determine" which two of these the Qur'an means, but argues that the gravest — the fourth and the sixth — best fit. It supports this with a long ḥadīth of Ḥudhayfah which it quotes from Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī. Ḥudhayfah asks the Prophet ﷺ about Bayt al-Maqdis and is told it was the most distinguished house of worship in the world, built for Sulaymān son of Dāwūd, peace be upon them, with gold, silver and precious stones gathered by the jinn whom Allah had made subject to him. When Ḥudhayfah asks where all that treasure went, the answer is that because they disobeyed, fell into sin and killed their noble prophets, Allah set Nebuchadnezzar over them, and his army stripped the sanctuary and enslaved them; then Allah raised up a king from among the kings of Persia who freed the remnant and had the valuables returned, warning them sternly that if they went back to disobedience and sin, killing and imprisonment would return upon them — which, the ḥadīth says, is the meaning of ayah 8. They did return to their old life, and Allah set the Roman emperor upon them — which is ayah 7.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reports the reading of Bayān al-Qur'an: the two episodes correspond to the breaking of two divine codes — first the law brought by Mūsā, then, after the coming of ʿĪsā, the law brought by him, peace be upon them. Its own commentary fills in the shape of each: in the first case "a disbelieving Magian monarch was made to sit over them," bringing great destruction; in the second, a Roman emperor "who killed and pillaged and made Baytul-Maqdis all demolished and rendered desolate."

## Ayah 6: the turn comes back round

*"Then We gave you a return of victory over them, and We helped you with wealth and children, and made you more numerous in manpower."*

Punishment was never the end of the story. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the pattern — on both occasions, when they repented of their misdeeds and resolved not to go near them again, Allah reinstated their country, their wealth and their children. The three things named in ayah 6 — property, offspring, numbers — are exactly what a defeated people lose. Restoration follows repentance as surely as ruin followed corruption.

## Ayah 7: the hinge of the whole passage

*"If you do good, you do good for your own selves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves."*

Allah states the rule the history is only evidence for. Ibn Kathir sets beside it: *"Whosoever does a righteous good deed, it is for the benefit of himself; and whosoever does evil, it is against himself"* (45:15). The Book of ayah 2 was a mercy to its holders, not a burden imposed on them — and abandoning it harmed no one but them.

Then the second collapse: *"…to disgrace your faces"* — Ibn Kathir: to humiliate you and subdue you — *"and to enter the Masjid"* — meaning Bayt al-Maqdis — *"as they had entered it before"*, just as the first invaders had entered the innermost parts of their homes — *"and to destroy with utter destruction all that fell in their hands."* Ibn Kathir explains the destroying as wrecking and inflicting ruin, and "all that fell in their hands" as everything they could get hold of.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that not only would enemies overrun their lives and property, but their qiblah, their sacred Bayt al-Maqdis, would not remain safe either — their disbelieving enemies would barge into it and defile and damage it, and that desecration was itself part of the punishment of its own guardians. This is the Masjid that Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī was told was the second house of worship set on earth, forty years after al-Masjid al-Ḥarām (reported by Muslim). A house that ancient and that honoured was not shielded by its own sanctity once its people abandoned the Book.

## Ayah 8: mercy held open, and a law left standing

*"Perhaps your Lord will have mercy on you — but if you return, We shall return. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers."*

"Perhaps your Lord may show mercy unto you" means, says Ibn Kathir, that He may rid you of them. And "if you return, We shall return" means: if you return to causing corruption, "We will once again punish you in this world, along with the punishment and torment We save for you in the Hereafter." Mercy is genuinely held open; the door back into punishment is left visibly unlocked.

**Hell as *ḥaṣīr*** — Ibn Kathir explains it as a place of permanent detention, a prison that cannot be avoided or escaped. The early scholars phrased it variously: Ibn ʿAbbās said *ḥaṣīr* here means a jail; Mujāhid said they will be detained in it; al-Ḥasan said it means a bed of Fire. Whichever image one takes, the shared sense is confinement with no exit — the exact opposite of the reprieve of ayah 6.

Qatādah applied the verse to the Prophet's ﷺ own era: the Children of Israel returned to aggression, so Allah sent this group against them — Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions — who made them pay the jizyah, in willing submission and feeling themselves subdued.

## The law did not expire with them

"If you return, We shall return" is a standing law, declared valid right through to the Day of Judgement. Its first addressees were the Children of Israel present in the Prophet's ﷺ own time, and to them it was a reminder: you were seized twice, once for opposing the code of Mūsā, once for opposing the code of ʿĪsā; this is now the period of the code of laws brought by Muhammad ﷺ, a period that lasts until the Last Day — so let those hostile to it not expect a different fate.

The purpose of narrating Israel's history in the Qur'an, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is to let Muslims understand that they are no exception to this divine law: their honour and ascendancy, their possessions and wealth, are inseparably tied to obedience to Allah; whenever they veer away from obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, their enemies are empowered to prevail over them — and then "the desecration of their places of worship will also not remain too far."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the loss of Bayt al-Maqdis in its own time by exactly this law, and says that the calamity, far from unsettling faith, "in reality… is confirming the Qur'an": Muslims forgot Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, ignored the life waiting for them in the Hereafter, and went scrounging for a share in the glamour of this world — and when they became strangers to the Qur'an and the Sunnah, the same divine law stood activated before them. Everything that came to pass, it concludes, came as the punishment of our own misdeeds. And it names one remedy only: that we feel ashamed of our misdeeds, make a genuine *tawbah* (repentance), start obeying the commandments of Allah, become true Muslims, and shun the grave sin of imitating and putting our trust in others — which is, in the end, exactly what ayah 2 asked of Israel: *take no wakīl besides Me.*

**Two qiblahs, two different laws.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that Allah made two places on earth a qiblah for those who worship Him — Bayt al-Maqdis and the Bayt Allah in Makkah — but the divine law relating to each differs. The protection of the Bayt Allah, so that disbelievers never take it over, Allah has taken upon Himself: the destruction of Abrahah al-Ashram, the Christian king of Yemen, together with his army and elephants before he could reach it — the event recorded in Sūrah al-Fīl — came as the result of that. No such guarantee attaches to Bayt al-Maqdis; as these ayat state, when its people go astray and indulge in disobedience it is snatched from them and passes into the control of disbelievers. Sanctity does not defend a place. Obedience does.

## Living it

- **Read ayah 7 as personal accounting.** Every good act is deposited to your own account and every wrong withdrawn from it. Ask of a deed not "who will know?" but "who is this actually going to?"
- **Guard the wakīl.** Faith is tested less by what you say you believe than by what you reach for when you are afraid. Ayah 2 makes reliance on Allah alone the purpose of revelation, not an optional refinement of it.
- **Take the door in ayah 6 seriously.** Repentance here is not merely forgiven; it is followed by the reinstating of country, wealth and children. No loss in this passage was final except where corruption resumed.
- **Say al-ḥamdu lillāh over small things.** Nūḥ, peace be upon him, is named in ayah 3 by his gratitude, and the ḥadīth reported by Imam Ahmad from Anas makes a mouthful of food, thanked for, a cause of Allah's pleasure. That is the trait his descendants were told to inherit.

passages.title: The Quran's guidance and human haste
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat place the Qur'an's own claim about itself beside a blunt fact about the people it was sent to. Ayat 9 and 10 tell us what the Book does — it guides to what is most upright, it carries good news to those who believe and act on it, and it warns those who deny the Hereafter. Ayah 11 then names the flaw that stands between a person and that guidance: he is in a hurry. The passage holds together as a contrast — a road laid out by the One whose knowledge is complete, offered to a creature who keeps his eyes on passing profit and loss.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the sequence. At the beginning of the surah, the majesty of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was described **through the miracle of al-Miʿrāj**. These present verses now cite **the miracle of the Qur'an as its confirmation**.

So one miracle is confirmed by another: the sign granted to the Messenger ﷺ, and then the sign he brought — the Book itself, which these verses now begin to praise.

## Ayah 9: "guides to that which is most upright"

Ibn Kathir opens his comment simply: **Allah praises His noble Book, the Qur'an, which He revealed to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. It directs people to the best and clearest of ways.**

The hinge of the ayah is one word — **aqwam**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "the most upright." Maʿārif unpacks it through Qurtubi, who explains aqwam as a way that has three qualities **at the same time**:

1. it is **closer to the destination**,
2. it is **easy**,
3. it is **free of dangers**.

That combination is the point. Maʿārif draws the conclusion out explicitly: the rules set for human life by the Holy Qur'an are **a combination of all three of these features together**.

Maʿārif then adds an honest caveat that is worth sitting with. **A person may, on occasion, start taking this way to be difficult or dangerous — but that is because of his own lack of comprehension**, not a defect in the road. And it grounds that in who is doing the guiding: the Lord of all the worlds has the most comprehensive knowledge of every single particle in the entire universe; before Him the past and the future are the same. He is the One who can have knowledge of the reality of what form and function are most beneficial for human beings. Man, by contrast, is unaware of things as they are in their comprehensive setting — and so, Maʿārif concludes, **he cannot identify even his own good or bad fully and decisively.**

That last sentence is the quiet key to the whole passage. Hold on to it; Maʿārif himself will return to it under ayah 11.

## Ayat 9–10: two announcements from one Book

Ibn Kathir reads the phrases of ayah 9 in a tight sequence, and each small qualifier matters:

- *"and gives good news to those who believe"* — **in it**, that is, in this Qur'an.
- *"those who do righteous deeds"* — **in accordance with it**.
- *"that they will have a great reward"* — **on the Day of Resurrection**.

So the good news is not for a vague goodwill toward scripture. It is for belief that settles on this Book and action that follows its shape. Belief and deed are named together, and the reward is located in the next world.

Ayah 10 turns to the other audience: *"those who do not believe in the Hereafter"* — for them, Ibn Kathir says, **a painful torment, likewise on the Day of Resurrection**. The ayah's own wording is *aʿtadnā* — "**for them We have prepared** a painful torment."

Ibn Kathir then places beside it a parallel verse: *"...then announce to them a painful torment"* (84:24). The verb there for "announce" — *fa-bashshirhum* — is the same verb used in ayah 9 for giving **good news**, *yubashshiru*. The Book that carries glad tidings to one group carries an announcement to the other in the identical grammatical breath — the same messenger, the same voice, two utterly different destinations. That is the shape of ayat 9 and 10 together: one Book, two announcements, and the dividing line named in the text is whether a person believes in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 11: the man who prays for his own ruin

And there the passage turns. *"And man invokes for evil as he invokes for good, and man is ever hasty."*

Ibn Kathir explains it as Allah telling us about **man's haste, and how he sometimes prays against himself, or his children, or his wealth** — praying for something bad to happen to them, or for them to die or be destroyed, invoking curses. And then the devastating line: **if Allah were to answer his prayer, he would be destroyed because of it.** Ibn Kathir supports this with 10:11, *"And were Allah to hasten for mankind the evil..."*, and reports that this is how the ayah was interpreted by **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah**.

Read the ayah again with that in mind. It does not say man prays for evil *sometimes*. It says he prays for evil **the way he prays for good**.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection back to ayah 9 himself. Having said that man cannot identify his own good or bad fully and decisively, he writes: **"Perhaps, it is based on this congruity that it was said in verse 11 that man would, on occasions, pray for something in a haste, something that spells out destruction for him."** The two halves of the passage are joined by that one incapacity — a creature who cannot reliably tell his own good from his own harm will sometimes ask, in all sincerity, for his own harm.

**A warning about the tongue.** In this context Ibn Kathir recalls the Prophet's ﷺ instruction — *"Do not pray against yourselves or your wealth, for that might coincide with a time when Allah answers prayers."* (Ibn Kathir refers back to an earlier discussion of this hadith rather than naming its source here, so it is passed on as he passes it on, without attributing it to a named collection.) The reasoning is quietly sobering: you do not know which moment is the answered one. And what makes the son of Adam speak that way, Ibn Kathir says, is **his anxiety and his haste** — hence the closing words of the ayah, *"and man is ever hasty."*

**The mercy in the delay.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the other side, and it is one of the most consoling notes in the passage: man will sometimes pray in haste for something that spells out destruction for him, and if Allah taʿālā were to answer such a prayer he would be ruined — **but Allah taʿālā does not answer such prayers instantly, until man himself comes to realise that his prayer was made in error and that it was fatal for him.** The unanswered duʿā is not neglect. On Maʿārif's reading, the delay is the space in which a person comes to see what he was really asking for.

## The haste of our father Adam

Right after the words *"and man is ever hasty,"* Ibn Kathir records what **Salmān al-Fārisī and Ibn ʿAbbās** mentioned about Adam. When his soul was breathed into him it entered his body from his head downwards. When it reached his brain he sneezed and said, *"Al-ḥamdu lillāh"* — and Allah said, *"May your Lord have mercy on you, O Adam."* When it reached his eyes, he opened them. When it reached his body and limbs, he began to stare at them in wonder. And then — before the soul had reached his feet — **he wanted to get up**. He could not. And he said, *"O Lord, make it happen before night comes."*

He wanted to rise before he had feet to rise on; even his request was a request to hurry. Ibn Kathir places the story here as an illustration of the very trait the ayah names.

## The standing rule

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that final clause as **a natural weakness of man stated in the form of a standing rule — that man is, by nature, haste-prone.** His description is uncomfortably accurate: man keeps his sight trained on passing profit and loss and **falls short on foresight and hindsight**. He loves to go for the immediate gain and comfort, even if it happens to be only a little, and **he would not bat an eye before preferring it to the greater and more lasting gain and comfort**. In short, says Maʿārif, the verse points to a natural weakness of human beings in general.

Set that against ayat 9 and 10 and the unit comes into focus:

- Ayah 9 offers a way that is nearer, easier and safer — **and its reward is a great reward on the Day of Resurrection**.
- Ayah 10 warns of a painful torment — **also on the Day of Resurrection**.
- Ayah 11 says the traveller is, by nature, a creature who prefers the smaller immediate good to the greater and more lasting one.

Both of the things the Book announces are dated to a day that has not yet come. And the weakness the Book names in the very next breath is precisely a weakness about things that have not yet come.

## A second view on ayah 11

Maʿārif also reports that **some authorities in tafsīr have taken this verse to be related to a particular event**: the prayer of **Naḍr ibn Ḥārith**, who in the heat of his hostility to Islam said, *"O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us rocks from the skies, or send upon us some other painful punishment."* On that reading, *al-insān* ("man") in the ayah refers to him **and those like him**.

Maʿārif gives the general rule about human nature first and then reports this occasion as what some scholars identified, with the phrase "or those like them" keeping the wider meaning in view; neither reading is presented as cancelling the other. And notice the wording either way: what Naḍr asked for was *ʿadhāb alīm*, a painful punishment — the same phrase ayah 10 uses for what awaits those who do not believe in the Hereafter. It is the clearest case imaginable of Maʿārif's point: a prayer made in haste which, had it been answered, would have been the man's ruin.

## Living it

**Guard your tongue in anger.** The clearest practical instruction in this passage is the Prophet's ﷺ warning not to pray against yourselves or your wealth — and Ibn Kathir's own gloss widens the picture to praying against oneself, one's children, or one's wealth. The curse muttered over a child who will not sleep, the "I wish I were dead" of a hard week, the wish that a business would just burn down: ayah 11 counts these as invocations, made the way you make your best ones, and the hadith says you do not know which hour is the answered one.

**Re-read your unanswered prayers.** Maʿārif's point deserves to change how you feel about them. Some duʿās are not answered at once, and the waiting is what lets a person come to see that the prayer was made in error and would have been fatal for him. That is not Allah ignoring you.

**When a ruling of the Book feels hard, suspect your own sight first.** Maʿārif is explicit that the difficulty comes from our own lack of comprehension, not from a flaw in a road that is aqwam — nearer, easier, safer — because it is charted by the One before whom past and future are the same.

**Lengthen your horizon.** The reward in ayah 9 and the punishment in ayah 10 are both placed on the Day of Resurrection. Every time you choose the smaller sooner thing over the greater and more lasting one, you are living out the weakness ayah 11 describes. Every time you don't, you are letting the Book do to you exactly what it says it does: guide you to what is most upright.

passages.title: Day, night, and the record round the neck
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take you from the sky to your own neck. Allah reminds us of the great signs He created — the alternation of night and day — and of what they are *for*: earning a living, and keeping count. Then, without pause, He tells you what is being counted. Time is not simply passing; it is being recorded. Ibn Kathir puts the join plainly: it is "after mentioning time, and the deeds of the son of Adam that take place therein" that Allah speaks of the record fastened to every neck. Ayah 12 gives you the clock; ayat 13–14 give you the ledger it has been keeping.

## Two signs, one obliterated and one made to shine

Ayah 12 opens: "And We have appointed the night and the day as two Ayat (signs). Then, We have obliterated the sign of the night (with darkness) while We have made the sign of the day illuminating."

Calling night and day *two* signs is already instructive: each is known by its own marks. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah made the night a sign having distinguishing features by which it is known — its darkness, and the appearance of the moon — and gave the day its own distinguishing features: the light, and the appearance of the shining sun. He made a distinction between the light of the moon and the light of the sun precisely so that the two may be told apart from one another, as in Allah's words, "It is He Who made the sun a shining thing and the moon a light and measured out for it stages that you might know the number of years and to count" (10:5).

The two verbs of ayah 12 are worth sitting with. The night's sign is *obliterated* — the ayah is rendered "obliterated (with darkness)." Against it stands the day's sign, *mubṣirah*, rendered "illuminating": the sign that hands the world back to your eyes.

The early authorities read the obliteration in more than one way, and the sources report more than one without forcing a choice. Ibn Jurayj reported that ʿAbdullah bin Kathir said it means "the darkness of the night and the twilight of the day." Ibn Jurayj also reported from Mujahid that "the sun is the sign of the day and the moon is the sign of the night," and that "We have obliterated the sign of the night" refers to the moon's blackness, "which is how Allah has created it." And Ibn Abi Najih reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said of the two signs: "By night and day, this is how Allah created them, may He be glorified." That last comment is a fence as much as an explanation: this is not damage or an afterthought. Allah made them so from the start.

## Why the night was made dark

The ayah states the purpose of the daylight, but as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the wisdom behind the making of the night dark is not mentioned in this place. It has, however, been mentioned in other verses: the darkness of the night is appropriate and conducive to sleep and rest. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something easy to miss — the divine arrangement is not merely that *you* sleep, but that humans and animals go to sleep in the darkness of that very night, the whole world sleeping simultaneously in harmony with its night. Had different people been scheduled to sleep at different timings, the noises made by those awake and those working at jobs would have turned the sleep of the sleeping into a nightmare. The darkness is a mercy that has to fall on everyone at once to work at all.

Ibn Kathir gathers the verses that make the same point from the other side — by asking what it would be like if the alternation stopped: "Say: 'Tell me! If Allah made the night continuous for you till the Day of Resurrection, which god besides Allah could bring you light?'… 'If Allah made the day continuous… which god besides Allah could bring you night wherein you rest?' It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the night and the day that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty — and in order that you may be grateful" (28:71–73). And: "He it is Who has put the night and the day in succession, for such who desires to remember or desires to show his gratitude" (25:61–62). The alternation is not a neutral mechanism; it is offered as a standing invitation to remember and to thank.

## Why the day was made bright: work and reckoning

Ayah 12 gives two purposes for the light: "that you may seek bounty from your Lord, and that you may know the number of the years and to count."

**Seeking bounty.** Ibn Kathir glosses this as "your living and travels" — going out, earning, doing your work. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the practical point that natural light is what jobs, businesses and industries actually need.

**Knowing the count.** Ibn Kathir lists what the count is for: so people know the number of days, weeks, months and years, and therefore the appointed times for paying debts, doing acts of worship, dealing with transactions, paying rents and so on. Then he adds the sentence that makes the whole sign visible: *if time stood still and never changed, we would not know any of these things.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works it out in the same key — the completion of three hundred and sixty days tells us a full year has gone by; without this variation of night and day it would have been difficult to fix the wages of the wage earner, the employment of the employee, and the time duration of transactions. Allah cites the crescents in the same spirit: "They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: 'These are signs to mark fixed periods of time for mankind and for the pilgrimage'" (2:189).

Notice what this does. The sky is presented as a measuring instrument. Debts, wages, contracts, worship — the entire structure of human obligation depends on a count that Allah, not man, set turning. Ayah 12 closes: "And We have explained everything (in detail) with full explanation." And having established that the universe is built to keep accounts, the passage turns to the account that matters most.

## What is fastened to the neck

Ayah 13: "And We have fastened every man's Ṭāʾirah (deeds) to his neck."

Ibn Kathir explains the word *Ṭāʾirah* — literally, something that flies — as referring to a man's deeds, which fly from him; this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others. Deeds fly from a person: done, out of the hand, seemingly beyond reach. The ayah says they are nonetheless fastened to him. It includes both good deeds and bad deeds, Ibn Kathir stresses, and a person will be forced to acknowledge them and will be rewarded or punished accordingly.

**Why the neck?** Ibn Kathir gives a precise reason: the neck is mentioned because it is a part of the body that has no counterpart, and when one is restrained by it, he has no escape. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the other half of the image: one's book of deeds stays with the doer no matter where or in whatever condition one is, and what he or she does continues to get recorded there.

That writing is continuous. Ibn Kathir cites: "the two receivers (recording angels) receive (each human being), one sitting on the right and one on the left. Not a word does he utter but there is a watcher by him ready (to record it)" (50:17–18); and "verily, over you are appointed angels to watch you, Kirāman Kātibīn — writing down (your deeds), they know all that you do" (82:10–12). Nothing is too small to make the page: "So whosoever does good equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it. And whosoever does evil equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it" (99:7–8). Ibn Kathir sums it up: the deeds of the sons of Adam are preserved, whether they are great or small, and they are recorded night and day, morning and evening — the very cycle ayah 12 just described. The clock and the ledger run on the same movement.

## A book you will find wide open

"…and on the Day of Resurrection, We shall bring out for him a Book which he will find wide open."

Ibn Kathir: all of a person's deeds will be collected for him in a Book which will be given to him on the Day of Resurrection — either in his right hand, if he is one of the blessed, or in his left hand if he is one of the wretched. Qatadah, in the report of Maʿmar, explains "We shall bring out for him" simply: "We shall bring forth those deeds."

And *manshūran* — "wide open." Ibn Kathir says it means it will be open for him and others to read all of his deeds, from the beginning of his life until the end. There is no editing stage, no private viewing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the sequence: the book stays with the doer through life; when death comes it is closed and set aside safely; and on the Day of Judgment it is placed in his own hand so that he would himself read it and himself decide whether he is deserving of reward or deserving of punishment.

## "Read your Book"

Ayah 14 is the one line of speech in the passage: "Read your Book. You yourself are sufficient as a reckoner against you this Day."

The force of it is that no external prosecutor is needed. Ibn Kathir's comment: you have not been treated unjustly, and nothing has been recorded against you except what you have done, because you remember everything that you have done, and no one will forget anything that he did. That is the meaning of "you yourself are sufficient as a reckoner." The evidence and the witness and the memory are all *you*. As Allah says, "On that Day man will be informed of what deeds he sent forward and what he left behind. Nay! Man will be a witness against himself, though he may put forth his excuses" (75:13–15).

And a mercy hidden in the command: how do you tell someone who never learned to read to *read*? Ibn Kathir answers that everyone will be able to read his Book, whether he is literate or illiterate. Qatadah is reported to the same effect in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — it will be a day when even an illiterate person will be able to read his book of deeds.

## Al-Hasan's words

Maʿmar said that al-Hasan recited "one sitting on the right and one on the left" (50:17) and then said:

> "O son of Adam, your Book has been opened for you, and two noble angels have been entrusted to accompany you, one on your right and one on your left. The one who is on your right records your good deeds, and the one who is on your left records your bad deeds. 'So do whatever you want, a lot or a little, until you die, then I will fold up your Book and tie it to your neck with you in your grave. Then when you come out on the Day of Resurrection, you will find the Book wide open, so read your Book.' By Allah, the One Who makes you accountable for your own deeds is being perfectly just."

Ibn Kathir's own verdict on this: "These are some of the best words Al-Hasan ever spoke, may Allah have mercy on him." Note the daring turn in the middle — "so do whatever you want" — which is not permission but the most sobering thing that can be said to a free person: the pen is running either way, so choose what you would like to read.

## Deeds that go missing from the page

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a warning here. Al-Isbahani has reported, on the authority of Sayyidna Abu Umamah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: on the Day of Qiyamah, when the book of deeds belonging to people will be given in their hand, someone will notice that some of his good deeds were not recorded there. He will tell his Lord about the particular deeds missing from there. His Lord will tell him that He had erased those deeds, for he used to speak ill of people behind their backs. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this through Mazhari; the report is given there without a named ḥadīth collection, so take the teaching and leave the attribution where the source left it.)

Set that beside Ibn Kathir's assurance that deeds are preserved, great or small. According to this report, backbiting does not merely add sins to the page — good deeds can be erased from it. The tongue reaches the record in both directions.

## Living it

The passage is short on commands and long on realism, and it changes a person mainly by changing how the ordinary day feels.

**Treat the daylight as capital, not scenery.** Ayah 12 says the day was made bright so you could seek bounty from your Lord. Earning, working, travelling — done for that reason, in that light, they are the very use Allah named.

**Let the count mean something.** The same alternation that lets you date a contract is dating you. Every completed cycle of night and day is one more entry closed.

**Assume the pen.** The angels are on the right and the left; speech is recorded as surely as action — "not a word does he utter but there is a watcher by him ready." Words are where most people's ledgers are quietly won and lost, which is exactly the point of the report about speaking ill of people behind their backs.

**Do your own reckoning first.** Since on that Day you will be sufficient as a reckoner against yourself, you already possess the instrument. Nothing stops you from opening the page tonight rather than waiting to find it wide open in public.

**And take the fairness seriously.** Nothing is recorded against you except what you did; not a speck of good is dropped. Al-Hasan's closing oath is the note to end on — the One who makes you accountable for your own deeds is being perfectly just.

passages.title: Each soul's burden and ruined nations
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat set out how Allah's justice works — first with the individual, then with whole nations. Ayah 15 gives two principles: every soul carries its own account and no one else's, and Allah punishes no one until a Messenger has come to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to exactly this as the thread joining them — the earlier verses state Allah's customary practice of not sending punishment upon a people until His commandments reach them through the prophets; ayat 16 and 17 give what happens on the other side, when the message of Allah and His Messenger *does* reach a people and they still show defiance.

## Guidance is something you keep; misguidance is a wound you inflict on yourself

Ibn Kathir reads the opening of ayah 15: whoever is guided and follows the truth, walking in the footsteps of the Prophet ﷺ, gains the good consequences of that **for himself**. And whoever goes astray — away from the truth, deviating from the way of guidance — is wronging himself and will have to bear the consequences. Guidance is not a favour you do for Allah, and rejection is not an injury you inflict on Him. Both return to the person who chose them.

## "No one laden with burdens can bear another's burden"

Ibn Kathir: no one will have to bear the sins of another, and he does not wrong anyone besides himself. He supports it with Allah's words elsewhere: "and if one heavily laden calls another to bear his load, nothing of it will be lifted" (35:15).

**An apparent problem, and its answer.** Other ayat say the misleaders "shall bear their own loads, and other loads besides their own" (29:13), and speak of "the burdens of those whom they misled without knowledge" (16:25). Is that not one person bearing another's burden? Ibn Kathir states there is no contradiction between this and those ayat. Those who called others to do evil will bear the sin of their own deviation as well as the sin of those whom they led astray — **without detracting the least amount from the burden of those people**, and none of this burden shall be removed from them. So no burden is ever *transferred*; the caller to evil simply has a second crime of his own. Ibn Kathir closes with a striking phrase: this is **"the justice and mercy of Allah towards His servants."** Justice, because the misleader does not escape what he set in motion. Mercy, because no one is ever charged for a sin he did not choose.

It cuts away every excuse built on other people — my family, my culture, my teachers, the era I was born into. And it cuts away every despair built on other people too: no one else's sin can be laid on you.

## "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger"

Ibn Kathir: out of His justice, Allah does not punish anyone until He has established proof against him by sending a Messenger to him. He gathers the ayat that show this principle playing out on the Day of Judgement — and in every one, the people condemned admit that they *were* warned:

- The keepers of Hell ask each group cast in, "Did no warner come to you?" and they answer, "Yes, indeed a warner did come to us, but we belied him and said: 'Allah never sent down anything (of revelation); you are only in great error'" (67:8–9).
- The keepers ask, "Did not the Messengers come to you from yourselves — reciting to you the verses of your Lord, and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?" They say: "Yes," but the Word of torment has been justified against the disbelievers (39:71).
- And when they cry out to be brought out so they may do righteous deeds, the reply comes: "Did We not give you lives long enough, so that whosoever would receive admonition could receive it? And the warner came to you" (35:37).

Ibn Kathir concludes that there are other ayat too which indicate that Allah will not make anyone enter Hell except after sending a Messenger to them.

## What about those the message never reached?

Ibn Kathir treats at length a question the scholars have discussed for centuries. What of children who die when they are little, and their parents are disbelievers? What of the insane, the deaf, the senile — and those who die during the circumstances of *Fatrah*, when no Message reached them? Ibn Kathir notes plainly that scholars "in earlier and modern times have disagreed" on this, and he prays Allah's mercy on them.

**The first hadith: the four who will argue their case.** Imam Ahmad reported from Al-Aswad bin Sariʿ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that there are four who will present their case on the Day of Resurrection: a deaf man who never heard anything, an insane man, a very old and senile man, and a man who died during the Fatrah. The deaf man will say, "O Lord, Islam came but I never heard anything." The insane man will say, "O Lord, Islam came and the young boys were throwing camel dung at me." The senile man will say, "O Lord, Islam came and I did not understand anything." And the one who died during the Fatrah will say, "O Lord, no Messenger from You came to me." Allah will accept their pledge of obedience to Him, then He will send word to them that they should enter the Fire. "By the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Muhammad, if they enter it, it will be cool and safe for them."

They are not condemned for a message they never received; they are given, on that Day, the test they never had in this life.

Ibn Kathir adds that there is a similar report with a chain from Qatadah, from Al-Hasan, from Abu Rafiʿ, from Abu Hurayrah, but ending: "Whoever enters it will find it cool and safe, and whoever does not enter it will be dragged into it." This was also recorded by Ishaq bin Rahwayh from Muʿadh bin Hisham, and by Al-Bayhaqi in *Al-Iʿtiqad*, with the comment, "This is a Sahih chain."

It was also reported by Ibn Jarir from the hadith of Maʿmar, from Hammam, from Abu Hurayrah, who attributed it to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayrah then said: "Recite, if you wish: *And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger*" — tying the hadith directly back to our ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that it was also narrated by Maʿmar from ʿAbdullah bin Tawus, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, but that route is *Mauquf*, not attributed directly to the Prophet ﷺ.

**The second hadith: children.** Ibn Kathir cites the teaching, reported from Abu Hurayrah without a collection being named here, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: every newborn is born in a state of *Fitrah* (the natural state of man), then his parents make him into a Jew or a Christian or a Zoroastrian, as animals produce whole animals: do you see any that is born mutilated, with something missing? According to one report, they said, "O Messenger of Allah, what about those who die when they are little?" He said: **"Allah knows best what they would have done."**

Imam Ahmad also reported from Abu Hurayrah — and here Ibn Kathir preserves an explicit uncertainty about the chain, "as far as I know; the narrator was not sure if it was attributed to Musa" — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The children of the Muslims are in Paradise, being taken care of by Ibrahim."

And in Sahih Muslim it is reported from ʿIyyad bin Hammad that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah said: "I have created My servants as *Hunafa*." According to another version, the wording is "as Muslims."

**The third hadith: the children of the idolaters.** In his book *Al-Mustakhraj ʿAla Al-Bukhari*, Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Barqani recorded the hadith of ʿAwf Al-Aʿrabi, from Abu Rajaʾ Al-ʿUtardi, from Samurah, that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Every newborn is born in a state of Fitrah." The people called out, "O Messenger of Allah! What about the children of the idolaters?" He said, **"And the children of the idolaters too."** At-Tabarani reported that Samurah said: "We asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the children of the idolaters, and he said, 'They are the servants of the people of Paradise.'"

**The fourth hadith.** Ahmad reported that Hasnaʾ bint Muʿawiyah, from Bani Suraym, said that his paternal uncle said to him: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who is in Paradise?' He said: 'Prophets are in Paradise, martyrs are in Paradise, infants are in Paradise, and baby girls who were buried alive are in Paradise.'"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Tafsir Mazhari draws the same conclusion straight from the wording of ayah 15: since no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another, the children of idolaters and disbelievers who die before reaching adulthood will not be punished — they do not deserve punishment on account of the denial and disbelief of their parents. Maʿārif also notes that the sayings of leading jurists differ about this issue.

**Why the scholars urged restraint.** Ibn Kathir is candid: to discuss this issue we need good, sound proof, but people who have no knowledge of the Shariʿah may try to speak about it anyway — and for this reason some of the scholars did not like to discuss it. He names Ibn ʿAbbas, Al-Qasim bin Muhammad bin Abi Bakr As-Siddiq, and Muhammad bin Al-Hanafiyyah among those from whom this view has been narrated.

Ibn Hibban recorded in his *Sahih* that Jarir bin Hazim said he heard Abu Rajaʾ Al-ʿUtardi say that he heard Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) say that, while he was on the Minbar, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "This Ummah will be fine so long as they do not talk about children and the divine decree." Ibn Hibban said this means talking about the children of the idolaters. Abu Bakr Al-Bazzar also recorded it via Jarir bin Hazim, then said: "A group narrated it from Abu Rajaʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas, but it is Mauquf."

So the honest position for a believer is: Allah's justice is guaranteed by ayah 15, the reports above give us real hope, the scholars differed on the details, and "Allah knows best what they would have done" is a complete and sufficient answer.

**A further difference among jurists.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records three positions on the reach of ayah 15. Some leading Muslim jurists rule that people whom the call of any prophet or messenger did not reach will not be subject to any punishment, despite their disbelief. Others hold that those who deny the Islamic beliefs that can be understood through reason — such as the existence of Allah and His Oneness — will be punished for that disbelief even if no call from a prophet or messenger reached them, though there will be no punishment for the usual acts of disobedience and sins without the prior call and transmission of the divine message by prophets. Still others interpret *rasul* ("Messenger") in this ayah in a general sense — whether a messenger or prophet, or human reason itself, for that too is in a way a messenger of Allah.

## Ayah 16: what ruin looks like before it arrives

The ayah is rendered here as "Whenever We intend to destroy a society, We command its elite," and by Ibn Kathir as: "And when We decide to destroy a town (population), *Amarna* those who live luxuriously. Then, they transgress therein, and thus the word (of torment) is justified against it. Then We destroy it with complete destruction."

**Why the word *Amarna* is discussed so much.** The plain sense of *Amarna* is "We commanded," and that immediately raises a problem. Ibn Kathir notes that the commentators differed over the meaning of this word:

1. It means "We send Our decree upon them" — as Allah says elsewhere, "Our decree reaches it by night or by day." Ibn Kathir: *Amarna* cannot mean "Our command," because Allah does not command or enjoin immorality.
2. It means that Allah subjugated them to commit immoral deeds, so that they deserved the punishment.
3. It means "We commanded them to obey Us, but they committed immoral sins, so they deserved punishment" — reported from Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, and also the view of Saʿid bin Jubayr.
4. "We gave power to the evil people, so they committed sin therein, and because they did that, Allah destroyed them with the punishment" — reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, who compared it to "And thus We have set up in every town great ones of its wicked people" (6:133). This was also the view of Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid and Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas.
5. "We increase their numbers" — reported by Al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and also the view of ʿIkrimah, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah; it was reported from Malik and Az-Zuhri as well.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up this word under its own heading, "Another Tafsir of this verse." It observes that the *qiraʾat* of the word differ. In one rendition, opted for by Abu ʿUthman an-Nahdi, Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-ʿAliyah and Mujahid, the word carries a doubled sound on the letter *mim*: read as *ammarna*, it means "We made affluent people leaders and rulers, who then sank in sin, and thus became the cause of punishment for the whole people." Another *qiraʾah*, credited to Sayyiduna ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas, reads it as *aamarna* and was explained by them in the sense of *aktharna*, "We increase the number of" — so that when Allah sends punishment on a people, its initial sign is that the number of the reckless rich is increased among them, and through their spate of sins they become the cause of the punishment descending upon the entire people.

Maʿārif draws the conclusion: **either way — the government of the affluent, or the sheer abundance of such people in a society — this is not something to be happy about; rather, it is a sign of divine punishment.** Drunk with the pleasures their affluence and influence can buy, they start caring less for anything else, disobey the will and command of Allah personally, and lead the trail for others to follow in their footsteps. In consequence comes the punishment of Allah.

## "Were they not helpless, then?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a doubt. A surface look at "when We intend" followed by "We command" could suggest that destroying those people was the divine purpose from the very beginning — that they were commanded to believe and obey through the prophets, and then their indulgence in sin was made the cause of punishment, all of it coming from Allah. Were they not then a helpless and excusable lot?

The answer given: Allah has given man reason and choice, and has determined the ways of reward and punishment. If someone elects to do nothing but what brings punishment, then it is the customary practice of Allah that He would activate the causes that bring that same punishment. So the real cause of the punishment they receive is nothing but their own resolve and determination to remain on the side of disbelief and sin — and since this is no simple passing intention, they cannot be helpless or excusable. This dovetails with ayah 15: each soul is answering for its own load.

## Living it: the responsibility that comes with wealth

By particularly mentioning affluent people who use their wealth to pursue a life of luxury, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the ayah indicates something about how societies actually work: the masses are naturally affected by the deeds and morals of the rich among them and of those who rule over them. When those people get used to misdeeds, the whole nation follows suit and takes to misdeeds as the only available norm of social survival.

The practical conclusion: **those whom Allah has blessed with wealth should be more concerned with the correction of their own deeds and morals** — lest they fall into the trap of a luxurious lifestyle, become heedless of self-correction, and make an entire nation go astray because of them. If that happens, the curse of the misdeeds that issue forth from their nation will fall on them too. Read alongside ayah 15 and Ibn Kathir's explanation there: such a person is not punished for someone else's sin, but for his own — for the trail he blazed and they followed.

## Ayah 17: the record of ruined nations, and a Lord who misses nothing

"And how many generations have We destroyed after Nuh!" Ibn Kathir reads this as a warning to the disbelievers of the Quraysh for rejecting Allah's Messenger Muhammad ﷺ: Allah destroyed other nations who rejected the Messengers after Nuh. The meaning, as Ibn Kathir gives it, is: "You disbelievers are not more dear to Allah than they were, and you have rejected the most noble of the Messengers and the best of creation, so you are more deserving of punishment."

Ibn Kathir also draws a quiet historical point from the words "after Nuh": this indicates that during the centuries between Adam and Nuh, humans were following Islam. He cites Ibn ʿAbbas: "Between Adam and Nuh there were ten generations, during all of which humans were following Islam." Corruption of belief came later — it was not humanity's original condition, a quiet echo of what the fitrah hadith says about each newborn.

**"And sufficient is your Lord as All-Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants."** The passage closes on two of Allah's names, *Khabir* and *Basir*. Ibn Kathir: this means He knows everything they do, good and evil, and nothing at all is hidden from Him, may He be glorified and exalted.

And note the word *sufficient*: He alone is enough. If nothing at all is hidden from Him, then ayah 15 is not a slogan but a description of a real ledger: every soul carrying exactly its own load, before a Lord from whom nothing was ever concealed.

passages.title: Whoever desires this world or the Hereafter
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat set two kinds of human being side by side — the one whose wanting is fixed on this quick, hurrying life, and the one who wants the Hereafter and works for it — and then say something that can unsettle you: Allah gives to both. That is what holds the passage together. Ayah 18 and ayah 19 name the two desires and where each one ends; ayah 20 says both parties are supplied from one and the same divine bounty; ayah 21 tells you to look at how unequally that bounty is spread out in this life, and then warns that the real gaps are the ones opening up in the next. Read as one unit, the passage moves from *what you want*, to *how you pursue it*, to *what Allah's giving does and does not prove*, to *where the differences between people finally land*.

## Two wantings, and a world named by its speed

The passage opens by naming this life not by its pleasures but by its pace. Ibn Kathir's rendering of *al-ʿājilah* is "the quick-passing (transitory enjoyment of this world)," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase "the immediate life herein," describing this first person as one who elects to go for "the readily available benefits" of his life in this world. So the world here is named by what it does: it is *available now*, and it *does not last*.

And the giving matches the wanting. The one who wants what is immediate is granted immediately — *ʿajjalnā lahu fīhā*, "We readily grant him what We will."

But the sentence does not stop there. It adds *mā nashāʾu li-man nurīd* — "what We will, for whom We like." Ibn Kathir draws out the point: **Allah tells us that not everyone who desires this world and its luxuries gets what he wants.** That is attained by those whom Allah wants to have it, and they get what He wills that they should get. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah *narrows down* the general statements made in other ayat. So even the man who has organised his whole life around this world does not set his own terms. Two decisions are not his: **how much**, and **to whom**.

**And afterwards.** *Thumma jaʿalnā lahu jahannam* — "then, afterwards, We have appointed for him Hell," which Ibn Kathir specifies means in the Hereafter. Three words then describe what that is:

- *yaṣlāhā*, "he will burn therein" — Ibn Kathir: "he will enter it until it covers him on all sides." Not a punishment applied from outside, but one he is inside of.
- *madhmūman*, "disgraced" — "blamed for his bad behaviour and evil deeds, **because he chose the transient over the eternal**." Notice where Ibn Kathir puts the blame: on the exchange itself. The man was not cheated. He got what he wanted, and the trade was the crime.
- *madḥūran*, "rejected" — "far away (from Allah's mercy), humiliated and put to shame." He wanted nearness to a thing that ends, and gets distance instead.

Set against this, ayah 19 answers point for point: another desire, another kind of effort, another verdict. The two ayat are built to be read together, and the commentators read them that way.

## Which wanting? The word Maʿārif fixes on

Before you apply ayah 18 to yourself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks you to look at exactly how the ayah words the wanting: *man **kāna yurīd** al-ʿājilah*.
